notes:
I've put together notes on Luke 4:23–44, but they have gaps. Two of my main sources, Enduring Word and Precept Austin, cut off before reaching this passage. I also ran out of searches before covering every verse. **I found nothing usable on vv. 42 and 44.** Coverage of vv. 24–29, 31–33, 37 and 43 is thin. I found nothing on these verses from the Pentecostal, Lutheran or Orthodox sites, nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, and almost nothing from the NET Bible notes.

---

**v. 23**
- **Traditional reading (Barnes):** The proverb was probably a common one. Its point is that a man who claims to heal others should first cure himself to show he can be trusted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-23.html
- **Calvin:** The meaning is that a physician should start with himself and his own people. The people of Nazareth complained that Jesus slighted his hometown while making other towns famous with his miracles. Calvin adds that Jesus blames them for the fact that he doesn't work miracles there. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-23.html
- **GotQuestions:** The proverb carries a demand for proof, something like "if you're the Messiah, prove it." It also resembles our saying "charity begins at home." https://www.gotquestions.org/physician-heal-thyself.html
- **Ellicott / Pulpit (quoting Plumptre):** Luke was a doctor, so it's fitting that only his Gospel has this proverb. It seems to have been Jewish, with no trace of it in Greek writers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-23.htm
- **Looking ahead to the cross:** Several older commentators note that the same taunt was thrown at Jesus on the cross: "He saved others; himself he cannot save." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-23.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET note):** The proverb reflects a "prove it to us" attitude. Because Capernaum miracles are mentioned before Luke tells of any, many scholars suspect Luke moved this scene earlier to show what Jesus' ministry was typically like. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php/verse.php?book=Luk&chapter=4&verse=23
- **Pulpit's contrasting view:** Pulpit thinks Luke placed the Nazareth visit in its right order, and that Matthew and Mark tell it out of sequence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-30.htm

**vv. 24–27**
- **Matthew Henry:** Israel could just as fairly have said "Physician, heal thyself" to Elijah and Elisha. Those prophets worked their miracles among Gentiles, while Jesus at least worked his among Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-23.html

**v. 28**
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** God's right to do as he wills makes proud people angry. They won't seek his favour his way, yet they resent others receiving what they themselves neglect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-30.htm

**v. 29**
- **A sermon on Precept Austin:** The people of Nazareth thought his claim was blasphemy, as if he'd lost his mind, so they drove him to the hill to throw him off. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-sermons
- **Piper:** For now Jesus was untouchable, because he would decide when he died (John 10:18). https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king

**v. 30 (traditions really differ here: was it a miracle?)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** God rescued Jesus by an extraordinary miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-30.html
- **Presbyterian (Barnes):** Most likely Jesus used divine power, by a word or a look, to calm their passions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-30.html
- **Methodist (Wesley):** Perhaps he became invisible, or perhaps they were overawed. **Clarke** says that either Jesus blinded them or overpowered them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-30.html
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** No supernatural rescue is required. Ellicott warns against reading miracles into the text and says calm righteousness can disarm a mob. **Pulpit** agrees it wasn't necessarily a miracle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-30.htm
- **Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith):** He actually disappeared from their sight. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-30.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The commentators agree Luke means a miracle that proved Christ's divinity, citing Ambrose and Thomas Aquinas. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-30.html
- **Gill:** The escape shows that when Jesus later died, he gave up his life freely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-30.htm

**vv. 31–32**
- **Piper:** "Authority" means Jesus spoke as one with the right to tell people what to believe about God. His subject, judging from v. 43, was the good news of the kingdom. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king

**vv. 33–34**
- **Piper:** Jesus' teaching itself provoked the demon to expose itself, and deliverance followed. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** It's ironic that demons knew who Jesus was while his own townspeople didn't. The demon even testified that Jesus was holy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-4/

**vv. 35–36**
- **Matthew Henry:** "Be silent" literally means "be muzzled." Jesus stopped the demon's mouth against its will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
- **Piper (Baptist):** Demons ignore God's moral commands but cannot resist his sovereign word. Jesus' word carries both authority and power. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king

**vv. 38–39**
- **High fever:** The Cambridge Bible says Luke uses the doctors' technical split between "great" and "little" fevers (Galen). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-38.htm
- **Peter was married:** Cambridge notes that Peter was a married man. Pulpit calls Christ's choice of a married man a lasting protest against the extreme asceticism the church later taught. That is a Protestant point; I didn't find a Catholic response. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-38.htm
- **"Rebuked the fever," three readings:**
  - Constable: we needn't assume a demon caused the fever; Luke may just be personifying it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-38.html
  - Meyer: the fever is pictured as a hostile, personal power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-38.htm
  - Calvin: diseases are God's messengers carrying out his judgments, and he recalls them when he pleases. https://ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.xxxix.htm
- **Piper:** Luke uses the same word "rebuke" as in v. 35 to show Jesus rules over nature as well as demons. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king
- **Matthew Henry:** Even homes Christ visits still suffer sickness. When relatives are ill, we should bring them to Christ in prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_004.cfm

**v. 40**
- **Guzik:** Jesus worked hard and put others' needs before his own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-4/
- **Piper:** Luke shows this was no one-off: Jesus has power over "various" diseases and "many" demons. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king

**v. 41 (several explanations for the silencing)**
- **Jesus wanted no apparent alliance with demons:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says he refused their testimony because accepting it would make him look allied with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
  - Matthew Henry: this made clear he had conquered them, not made a deal with them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
  - Catholic (Haydock) agrees: he wanted no suspicion of any understanding with evil spirits. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
- **Satan should not be heard even when telling the truth:** Geneva Study Bible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-41.htm
- **Popular expectations and timing:**
  - Barclay: people expected a conquering Messiah, and the country was close to revolt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
  - Coffman: it was too early to announce he was the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/4-41.html
  - Piper: the common idea of the Messiah had no cross in it. Luke 9:20–22 shows Jesus had to suffer first. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king
- **Text note:** Older manuscripts leave out "Christ" in the demons' cry, reading only "Thou art the Son of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/4-41.htm

**v. 43**
- **Piper:** "The other towns as well" shows the kingdom message was what Jesus had been preaching in Capernaum too. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-demons-the-fever-and-the-word-of-the-king
